summary: Part 1 of the Indigenous histories split: Ethnohistory and Indigenous–newcomer relations extended to 2024. Four part-1 strands move out of Indigenous history with their ids (middle_ground to ethnohistory; colonial_geography, native_newcomer_institutions and indigenous_labour_exchange to native_newcomer); White, Sandlos and Spence's rows move; the indigenous rows of Harris, J. R. Miller, Cronon, Jacoby and Richter are removed because each already has a row in the receiving field. Five edges are rerouted, none removed: edge_909 (White) and edge_1437 (Richter) to ethnohistory, edge_777 (Harris) and edge_1253 (conservation) to native_newcomer, edge_1242 (Cronon) to environment; edge_1231 (Wolfe) is kept. Ethnohistory gains the middle-ground debate in its participants' words: DuVal, Hämäläinen and Witgen as read by named reviewers (three critique arrows against White) and White's 2021 self-critique of ethnohistory, paraphrased from the Portuguese translation; native_newcomer gains Andersen's critique of 'mixedness' (his own words) and three new strands (treaties; parks, game laws and dispossession; the field's accounts of itself). Four edges requested by Agent B (Audra Simpson and McNickle to ethnohistory; LaRocque twice to native_newcomer) are drafted here. New descriptions, scope notes, date labels, coverage to 2024, and 33 chronology events (15 + 18).

Every stage-1 edge rests on the author's own words read (Andersen's introduction; White's interview, paraphrased) or on a named reader's explicit statement read in full (Piker extract, Hatfield, Isaac, Grillot, Reda). Endpoint reroutes, each guarded: edge_909 and edge_1437 follow their work into ethnohistory/middle_ground; edge_777 follows Harris's moved strand; edge_1253 goes to the new native_newcomer/conservation_dispossession strand (settler scholarship about dispossession); edge_1242 (Cronon's wilderness essays) goes to environment/conservation_dispossession, where his same sentence already stands, because his essays are US environmental history, not Indigenous-authored history and not Canadian relations historiography (Cronon's indigenous row, which carried edge_1242, is removed; his environment row stays). edge_1231 (Wolfe → indigenous/settler_colonial_interlocutor) is kept, with Wolfe's indigenous row: its evidence is two Native American and Indigenous Studies scholars' testimony (Goeman 2016, Kauanui 2016) about his engagement with their field, which is part-2 matter; Agent B owns that strand's text and may retitle it. Not done here and needed from others: (1) Agent B's chris_andersen node, people record and ihb_andersen_metis_2014_sample, on which ihA_rel_06 and the Andersen roster row depend; (2) Agent C's ihc_cha_2021 and ihc_fraser_stevenson_2022, cited in a new strand and two chronology events; (3) the indigenous/land strand keeps O'Brien and still lists Cronon, Spence, Jacoby and Sandlos in person_ids with their sources: no operation removes strand members, so the coordinator (or B, who owns the strand text) must decide; (4) John Lutz's indigenous row (labour and Stó:lō field school) is left for Agent C to move with stolo_community_university; (5) strand_redirects for the four moved strand addresses (indigenous/middle_ground → ethnohistory/middle_ground, and three to native_newcomer) are not expressible in this fragment; (6) the Ethnohistory principal-venue edge reroute is the coordinator's; strand redirects and claim-catalogue addresses for the moved strands come from the merge script. Corrections used: 'The Shapes of Power' is a chapter (Contested Spaces of Early America, 2014); the Van Kirk crosswalk count is not used. John Lutz's indigenous row is removed (roster_removals): he keeps rows in native_newcomer and in Agent C's community_engaged_indigenous, which carries the field school. Edges from other agents ending in A's fields: Agent C's ihC_rel_05 (community_engaged_indigenous → native_newcomer), ihC_rel_12 (Wheeler → native_newcomer/indigenous_critiques_of_framing), ihC_rel_16 (Macdougall → native_newcomer/fur_trade_families_metis) and ihC_rel_18 (Innes → native_newcomer/indigenous_critiques_of_framing) are accepted as drafted; none duplicates or contradicts A's: ihC_rel_16 runs parallel to ihA_rel_06 (Macdougall on race over culture, Andersen on mixedness against peoplehood; different authors, same strand, both kept). text_revisions.old: Combines historical and anthropological inquiry through archives, material evidence, language, oral traditions and situated cultural interpretation. North American claims research, Wendat/Huron historical reconstruction, Nahua documentary studies and Andean historical anthropology form distinct programmes. Ethnohistory studies historical change rather than assigning some peoples to an unchanging ethnographic past.
text_revisions.new: Combines historical and anthropological inquiry through archives, material evidence, language, oral traditions and situated cultural interpretation. North American claims research, Wendat/Huron reconstruction, Nahua documentary studies and Andean historical anthropology form distinct programmes. In the Great Lakes, White's The Middle Ground (1991) found accommodation in the long periods when 'whites could neither dictate to Indians nor ignore them'. From 2006 critics set his case inside a wider field of Native power: for DuVal 'only relatively weak people desired the kind of compromises inherent in a middle ground' (2006); Hämäläinen's Comanches left little room for one (2008); Witgen held that European possession of the interior 'never occurred' (2012). White replied that a middle ground needs 'a rough balance of power' (2006), and in 2021 granted that the agency argument could go too far. Ethnohistory studies historical change rather than assigning some peoples to an unchanging ethnographic past.

text_revisions.old: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and European newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, schools, missions, health and labour. Innis’s Fur Trade in Canada (1930) was subtitled ‘an introduction to Canadian economic history’. From the 1970s historians, geographers and archaeologists recast it with Indigenous people as actors: trappers, hunters and middlemen (Ray 1974), wives and kin in fur-trade society (Van Kirk; Brown, both 1980), and Wendat history across contact (Trigger 1976, 1985; Delâge 1985), while Dickason studied European representations of them (1984). The field long called itself ‘native–newcomer’ history, after Trigger’s Natives and Newcomers (1985); current usage prefers ‘Indigenous’. Miller (1989) offered a national synthesis of ‘Indian–white relations’. Later work studied reserve farming and policy (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), health (Kelm 1998) and wage labour (Lutz 1992). Brownlie and Kelm (1994) asked whether agency-centred work on Indian policy and the potlatch law (Cole and Chaikin; Miller; Loo) had made Native agency a colonialist alibi. Indigenous scholars questioned the framing: Sioui (1989) found conventional history without a method for Indigenous self-interpretation; Winona Stevenson (Wheeler) (1998) argued that historians of ‘Indian–White relations’, relying on one side’s records, kept even agency-centred work within a colonialist framework and set oral history aside; LaRocque (1999) found that the cross-cultural ethnohistory of Trigger, Brown and Van Kirk still ‘othered’ its subjects. After 2000, settler-colonial analysis read this history as continuing dispossession; Greer replied that the fur trade’s commercial penetration was a different form of invasion.
text_revisions.new: A Canadian historiography of relations between Indigenous peoples and newcomers, centred first on the fur trade and then on policy, treaties, schools, missions, health and labour. Innis (1930) made the fur trade 'an introduction to Canadian economic history'; from the 1970s Ray, Van Kirk, Brown and Trigger recast it with Indigenous people as actors, and Trigger's Natives and Newcomers (1985) gave the field its older name. Later work studied reserves (Carter 1990), residential schools (Miller 1996; Milloy 1999), treaties (Ray, Miller and Tough 2000), health (Kelm 1998), labour (Lutz), voyageurs (Podruchny 2006), authenticity (Raibmon 2005) and Stó:lō historical consciousness (Carlson 2010). Critics questioned the frame: Brownlie and Kelm on agency as alibi (1994), Wheeler (1998) and LaRocque (1999) on its reliance on one side's records, Andersen on reading Métis through 'mixedness' rather than peoplehood (2014). In 2010 Peers and Podruchny wrote that the field had moved 'far beyond older narratives'; in 2021 the CHA Council said historians had 'contributed in lasting and tangible ways' to Canada's refusal to face this history.

text_revisions.old: Cultural interaction exceeds a simple assimilation/persistence account. Great Lakes circumstances do not supply a universal account of colonization.
text_revisions.new: White's The Middle Ground (1991) found accommodation in the pays d'en haut, 1650–1815, created by 'a process of mutual invention by both the French and the Algonquians' (p. 50). From 2006 historians set it inside a wider field of Native power. The William and Mary Quarterly forum (2006: Sleeper-Smith, White, P. Deloria, Bohaker, Rushforth, Desbarats) examined its uses and limits (essays unread). DuVal held that 'only relatively weak people desired the kind of compromises inherent in a middle ground' (2006, as quoted by Piker and Isaac); Grillot reads Hämäläinen as leaving 'little or no middle ground for compromise' (2008); Reda reads Witgen as showing the French moving from misunderstanding to delusion (2012). Richter's Facing East (2001) and Calloway's continental history turned the view westward from Native communities. White set out the conditions, 'a rough balance of power, mutual need … and an inability by either side to commandeer enough force to compel the other to change' (2006, as quoted by Avila), and in a 2021 interview (published in Portuguese translation) became more critical of ethnohistory as a hybrid. Moved from Indigenous history in revision 1.201.

text_revisions.old: Women and kinship (Van Kirk) and company families (Brown) recast fur-trade society in 1980; Peterson and Brown’s collection treats Métis peoples in their own right (1985). Podruchny (2006) and Macdougall (2010) carry the strand past 2000.
text_revisions.new: Women and kinship (Van Kirk) and company families (Brown) recast fur-trade society in 1980; Peterson and Brown’s collection treats Métis peoples in their own right (1985). Podruchny (2006) and Macdougall (2010) carry the strand past 2000. Andersen (2014) criticised 'the simplistic tropes of mixedness and hybridity that seem to fascinate so many scholars who write of Métis histories' and located Métis peoplehood in a Red River historical core. Brown had written that 'there is no single Metis core identity but rather a range along a spectrum' (as translated by Peers and Podruchny, 2010) and in 2017 named The New Peoples and Andersen's book as the older and newer poles of the field.

field_sets.expect: The field overlaps with Indigenous history but does not automatically confer Indigenous authority, community consent or decolonizing method. Claims research could serve governments as well as claimants. Indigenous authors appear here as qualified interlocutors and critics, not as members of an externally assigned school. Lurie herself disputes restricting the approach to particular peoples. The Americas dominate this initial selection; Vansina provides a comparison with African oral-tradition methodology, not proof that African history descends from US ethnohistory.
field_sets.value: The field overlaps with Indigenous history but does not automatically confer Indigenous authority, community consent or decolonizing method. Claims research could serve governments as well as claimants. Indigenous authors appear here as qualified interlocutors and critics, not as members of an externally assigned school. Lurie herself disputes restricting the approach to particular peoples. The Americas dominate this initial selection; Vansina provides a comparison with African oral-tradition methodology, not proof that African history descends from US ethnohistory. Extended to 2024 in revision 1.201 (Indigenous histories split, part 1). The middle-ground debate is read through White's own statements (1991 excerpts; 2006 and 2011 as quoted; a 2021 interview published in Portuguese translation) and through named readers of DuVal (Piker, Hatfield, Isaac), Hämäläinen (Grillot) and Witgen (Reda); the 2006 WMQ forum essays and the DuVal, Hämäläinen, Witgen and Blackhawk introductions are unread. The American Society for Ethnohistory and its journal continue; selected presidential addresses after 2008 (Calloway, O'Brien, Shoemaker, Mundy) examine the field's categories and archives (abstracts only) and are dated as context, not as the field's centre. Indigenous historians on this roster also appear in Indigenous history where their own statements warrant it; no identity classification is recorded here. History PhD citation graph, release 2026-10-23: in Canadian History PhDs White is cited by 171 theses (7.0% of 2000–09 theses, 10.4% of 2018–25).

field_sets.expect: A research field in mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian historiography, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology and anthropology. It is not the atlas’s Indigenous history entry, which centres Indigenous historical traditions, community knowledge and authority. Several people sit in both (Dickason, Miller, Lutz, Trigger); their existing contexts are kept, and Indigenous historical practice is not subsumed here. It is not Settler colonialism, which reads dispossession as a continuing structure: most works here predate that framework, and whether any adopts it was not checked; and Greer’s critique points the other way. Indigenous critiques of the ‘relations’ framing (Sioui, LaRocque; Fixico and S. Miller in the US) appear as critics, not members, and the roster records no identity classification. Francophone work is thin in this selection (Delâge, Sioui); New France encounter history overlaps with Quebec historiography. The label keeps the field’s word ‘newcomer’ but uses ‘Indigenous’; ‘native–newcomer’, Trigger’s 1985 term, is explained in the description as the field’s historical name. ‘Indigenous–settler’ is avoided so as not to collide with Settler colonialism.
field_sets.value: Part 1 of the Indigenous histories family (revision 1.201): mostly academic, mostly non-Indigenous Canadian scholarship about Indigenous–newcomer relations, built on company, church and state archives together with archaeology, anthropology and, increasingly, oral history. Indigenous-authored history and critique (Indigenous history) and community-engaged research are separate entries; Indigenous critics of the 'relations' framing (Sioui, Wheeler, LaRocque, Andersen; Fixico and S. Miller in the US) appear here as critics, not members, and the roster records no identity classification. The settler-scholar approaches formerly housed in Indigenous history (Miller's syntheses, Lutz's labour history, Harris's colonial geography, settler work on conservation and dispossession) now sit here. It is not Settler colonialism, which reads dispossession as a continuing structure; after 2000 settler-colonial analysis read this history as continuing dispossession, and Greer replied that commercial penetration was a different form of invasion. Francophone work is thin (Delâge, Sioui) and was not surveyed after 2000. The label keeps the field's word 'newcomer' but uses 'Indigenous'; 'native–newcomer', Trigger's 1985 term, is the field's historical name. Extended to 2024: Peers and Podruchny 2010 and Andersen 2014 introductions read; Podruchny 2006, Raibmon 2005, Carlson 2010 and Brownlie and Kelm 1994 unread in the body. strand.title: Parks, game laws and dispossession
strand.focus: Settler historians of conservation: Binnema and Niemi (2006) on the Stoney excluded from Banff for game, sport, tourism and assimilation; Sandlos (2007) on northern game laws and sanctuaries as the state's authority over Dene and Inuit hunting; Spence (1999) on Indian removal and the national parks as the United States comparison. Carried over from Indigenous history's 'Land' strand in revision 1.201; O'Brien's Natick history stays there. The environment entry carries the same scholarship in its own strand.
strand.works: Spence, Dispossessing the Wilderness (1999); Binnema and Niemi (2006); Sandlos, Hunters at the Margin (2007)

strand.title: Treaty histories
strand.focus: Ray, Miller and Tough's history of the Saskatchewan treaties draws 'on a wide range of documentary sources' to show how the treaties were shaped by Hudson's Bay Company diplomacy, eastern treaty practice and western change, and why misunderstandings and disputes followed (2000, publisher's description). Miller's general history of treaty-making followed (2009).
strand.works: Ray, Miller and Tough, Bounty and Benevolence (2000); Miller, Compact, Contract, Covenant (2009)

strand.title: The field's accounts of itself after 2000
strand.focus: In 2010 Peers and Podruchny called Aboriginal history 'one of the most significant changes in Canadian historiography since the 1970s', said it had 'moved far beyond older narratives', and criticised archive-only work for 'shallow ethnocentric interpretations'; Brown's collected essays (2017) revisit her own terms. In 2021 the Canadian Historical Association's Council stated that historians 'have often been reticent to acknowledge this history as genocide' and had 'contributed in lasting and tangible ways' to Canada's refusal to come to grips with it. In 2022 Fraser and Stevenson evaluated 'the foundations of professional historical writing in Canada' in the light of the TRC (abstract).
strand.works: Peers and Podruchny, eds., Gathering Places (2010); Brown, An Ethnohistorian in Rupert's Land (2017); CHA Council statement (2021); Fraser and Stevenson, CHR (2022)

strand.title: Historical consciousness in ethnohistorical history
strand.focus: Carlson's study of Stó:lō identity combines, in Knickerbocker's words, 'a long historical view with a micro-ethnohistorical lens' and 'extensive use of oral history interviews' with Aboriginal and non-Aboriginal archives (2010). It rests on two decades of work with the Stó:lō; the community–university practice itself belongs to Community-engaged research.
strand.works: Carlson, The Power of Place, the Problem of Time (2010)
